newsitem.title: USA: CBOT traders say USDA crop data bearish wheat, soy.
newsitem.headline: CBOT traders say USDA crop data bearish wheat, soy.

text.p: CBOT traders said crop production and supply/demand data issued by USDA was bearish for wheat and soybeans, with corn seen opening lower on spillover selling.
There were early calls for wheat to open around two to three cents a bushel lower, soybeans down three to five cents and corn one to two cents weaker.
USDA estimated this year's U.S. winter wheat production at 1.604 billion bushels, slightly higher than the average projection in a Reuter survey of analysts of 1.579 billion.
"The wheat production number is bigger than the trade thought," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.
USDA put hard red winter output at 921 million, soft red at 422 million and winter white at 260 million. The average analysts projections were 899 million, 413 million and 267 million, respectively.
"The wheat number on balance is a little negative because the all wheat number was above average," a trader said.

USDA also raised its estimate for 1996/97 soybean ending stocks by five million bushels to 130 million. Analysts had expected the soybean ending stock number to be either left unchanged or raised by five million.
"The bean carryout went up so that is negative (for prices)," said Don Roose of U.S. Commodities.
USDA also left unchanged its estimates for Brazilian soybean prodution at 26.50 million tonnes.
"All in all it's pretty negative, said one floor trader. "They didn't lower the Brazilian crop and they raised the bean carryout."
USDA cut Argentine soybean production by 400,000 tonnes to 12.00 million tonnes. Some had expected a larger cut, possibly down to 11.50 million.
Roose cautioned, however, that higher than expected weekly new crop soybean export sales data, also issued by USDA early Thursday, would temper any losses in new crop.
USDA put weekly new crop soybean sales at 572,400 tonnes. Analyst estimates had ranged from 200,000 to 400,000 tonnes.
Favorable weather for fledgling corn and soybean crops in the U.S. Midwest was seen possibly adding to the downward pressure on prices in early trade, analysts said.
